title: Khao Sam Kaeo, a Port Between Oceans
place: Khao Sam Kaeo, near Chumphon, Thailand
text: Near today's Chumphon, a busy port city was active from the 4th century BCE to the 1st century CE. Archaeologists dug 136 test pits and found earthen walls, ramparts and water-control works around at least 35 hectares. Its stone, glass and copper crafts used techniques from India, Indian artisans may have worked there, and two seals with Chinese writing hint at Han merchants.

source.name: NUS Press, Southeast Asian Site Reports: Favereau and Bellina, Cultural Dynamics in the Early Multi-ethnic Ports of the Upper Thai-Malay Peninsula

title: A King Who Meditates in Stone
text: Jayavarman VII began his reign in 1181, after a troubled period that ended in 1177 with a Cham siege of Angkor. He made Mahayana Buddhism the state religion. His sandstone portraits show a mature man in humble meditation, eyes lowered and smiling calmly, with no royal insignia at all, a very human face for a mighty king.

source.name: Musée Guimet: Portrait of King Jayavarman VII

title: Koh Ker, the Rival Capital
text: In 921 King Jayavarman IV founded a new capital about eighty kilometres northeast of Angkor. The two cities co-existed as rival capitals until 928, then Koh Ker ruled alone until 944. Its builders used huge single blocks of stone, and its sculptors created the bold, lively Koh Ker Style, which shaped Khmer art long after the court moved back to Angkor.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Koh Ker, Archaeological Site of Ancient Lingapura or Chok Gargyar

title: The Temple in the Rich Forest
place: Sambor Prei Kuk, Kampong Thom, Cambodia
text: Sambor Prei Kuk, 'the temple in the richness of the forest', was Ishanapura, capital of the Chenla kingdom in the late 6th and early 7th centuries. Its 186 brick temples include rare octagonal shrines thought to show the flying palace of the god Indra. Inscriptions in Sanskrit and Old Khmer name kings and other individuals, and its style paved the way for Angkor.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Temple Zone of Sambor Prei Kuk, Archaeological Site of Ancient Ishanapura

title: The Stone Citadel of the Hồ
text: Built in 1397 between the Ma and Bưởi rivers, the Hồ Dynasty citadel was Vietnam's capital from 1398 to 1407. Its inner walls are made of huge limestone blocks, and its site was chosen by geomantic rules between two mountains. The citadel shows how Confucian ideas of royal power were taking hold in a mainly Buddhist country.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Citadel of the Ho Dynasty

title: A Sacred Axis From Mountain to Mekong
text: On the Mekong in southern Laos, the planned city of Shrestrapura grew up from the 5th century CE beneath Phou Kao mountain, also called Lingaparvata. Between the 5th and 15th centuries temples, shrines, reservoirs and a road to Angkor were laid out along a line about 10 kilometres long, from mountaintop to riverbank, to express Hindu ideas about nature and humanity. Vat Phou temple sits at its heart.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Vat Phou and Associated Ancient Settlements within the Champasak Cultural Landscape

title: Boundary Stones on Phu Phrabat
text: When Buddhism reached the Khorat Plateau in the 7th century, people began setting up sīma stones to mark sacred ground for monks. Phu Phrabat keeps the world's largest group of these Dvaravati-period stones still in place. The same rock shelters already held much older paintings of people, hand prints, animals and patterns, made by prehistoric visitors about two thousand years ago.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Phu Phrabat, a testimony to the Sīma stone tradition of the Dvaravati period

title: Si Thep's Dancing Statues
text: Si Thep, a moated twin town of the Dvaravati world, flourished in central Thailand from the 6th to the 10th centuries. More than 112 monastery sites have been found there, and Hindus and Buddhists of two schools lived side by side. Its sculptors made free-standing figures in the swaying Tribhanga pose, full of body movement, and nearby Khao Thamorrat is a rare Mahayana Buddhist cave monastery.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: The Ancient Town of Si Thep and its Associated Dvaravati Monuments

title: Monks Shipwrecked for a Fresh Start
text: King Dhammaceti of Pegu, called from the monastery to the throne, sent twenty-two senior monks to Sri Lanka to be re-ordained on the Kalyani River near Colombo. One ship was wrecked at Colombo and its party was shipwrecked again, and several monks died on the way home. In 1476 the king recorded the story on ten stone slabs, in Pali and Mon.

source.name: Government Printing, Burma (1892): The Kalyani Inscriptions Erected by King Dhammaceti at Pegu in 1476 A.D., Text and Translation

title: A Craftswoman Signs Her Jar
place: Chu Đậu, Nam Sách, Hải Dương, Vietnam
text: A blue-and-white jar now in the Topkapı Palace Museum in Istanbul carries an inscription naming the craftswoman Bùi Thị Hý and dating it to 1450, the 8th year of the Đại Hòa era. Chu Đậu village, where such wares are thought to have been made, was Vietnam's largest ceramics centre, producing pots for worship, home use and export.

source.name: National Museum of Vietnamese History: The cobalt blue pattern ceramic jar with swan decoration, an object recognized as Vietnam National Treasure

title: A Calendar Born in 638
text: Four burial urns found at Sri Ksetra in 1911 carry short Pyu inscriptions naming lords and the years they died. Historian Tilman Frasch argues that the dates most likely count from the Pyu–Myanmar era of 638 CE. That same Myanmar era has since been used for dating practically everything written in Myanmar, from inscriptions and manuscripts to printed books and newspapers.

source.name: Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society (Cambridge): Tilman Frasch, Pyu urns, Indian calendars, and Myanmar culture

title: A Woman in a Boat-Shaped Coffin
place: Ban Non Wat, Nakhon Ratchasima, Thailand
text: At Ban Non Wat, the first Bronze Age graves were dug much deeper than older ones. In Burial 569 a young to mid-aged woman lay in a wooden coffin with a pointed prow like a boat. She wore 2,382 shell beads and a marine shell bangle, fourteen pots surrounded her, and a socketed copper-base axe rested on her left shoulder.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): Charles Higham, Aggrandisers and the first copper-base metallurgy in Southeast Asia

title: Myanmar's Bronze Age Begins
text: On the edge of an old volcanic crater near the Chindwin River lies the Nyaung'gan cemetery. People here were buried with pottery, stone beads and bracelets, shell beads, spindle whorls, cattle bones and even a dog. New radiocarbon dates by a Myanmar and French team suggest the shift from stone to copper and bronze happened here in the tenth to ninth centuries BCE.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): Pryce et al., A first absolute chronology for Late Neolithic to Early Bronze Age Myanmar: new AMS 14C dates from Nyaung'gan and Oakaie

title: A Child With Roots in India
place: Vat Komnou cemetery, Angkor Borei, Takéo, Cambodia
text: A boy aged five to seven was buried at the Vat Komnou cemetery at Angkor Borei sometime between 78 and 234 CE. When scientists read his ancient DNA, they found that about 40 to 50 percent of his ancestry came from South Asia, mainly southern India. It shows that people from South Asia were already mixing with local families in Cambodia that early.

source.name: Scientific Reports (via PMC): Changmai et al., Ancient DNA from Protohistoric Period Cambodia indicates that South Asians admixed with local populations as early as 1st–3rd centuries CE

title: A Toolkit Carried to the Delta
text: Rạch Núi, a Neolithic village in the Mekong Delta, had no stone of its own. Yet archaeologists found a small, portable sandstone grinding stone there, used to polish and repair stone adzes, which probably came from a quarry more than 80 kilometres away. It hints at specialist tool makers or travelling traders, part of a trade network that moved goods over hundreds of kilometres.

source.name: Australian National University, College of Arts and Social Sciences: Archaeologists uncover ancient trading network in Vietnam

source2.name: Antiquity (Cambridge): Frieman et al., Rach Nui: ground stone technology in coastal Neolithic settlements of southern Vietnam

title: Halin Falls to Nanzhao
text: The Pyu kingdom flourished in central and northern Burma from the early centuries CE until around 832, when its capital Halin was sacked by forces of the Nanzhao kingdom from southern China. Halin was one of three brick-walled, moated Pyu cities, where people built Buddhist stupas, stored the ashes of the dead in urns and managed water to farm the dry zone.

source.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History: Kurt Behrendt, The Mon-Dvaravati Tradition of Early North-Central Thailand

source2.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Pyu Ancient Cities

title: Champa Strikes Back at Angkor
text: Champa, with its powerful fleet, had been conquered by the Khmer king Suryavarman II in 1145, but a new Cham king threw off Khmer rule two years later. In 1177 his successor struck back and sacked Angkor, the Khmer capital. The siege ended a troubled period for Cambodia and opened the way for the reign of Jayavarman VII.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Champa, ancient kingdom, Indochina

source2.name: Musée Guimet: Portrait of King Jayavarman VII

title: Raiders, Traders and a Chinese Fleet
text: Champa, the kingdom of the Cham people on Vietnam's central coast, had a powerful fleet used for both trade and piracy. Around 400 it was united under King Bhadravarman. In 446 the Chinese invaded in revenge for Cham raids on their coast and brought Champa under their overlordship, until a new dynasty threw off that allegiance in the 6th century.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Champa, ancient kingdom, Indochina

title: Đại Việt Pushes South
text: Short of farmland in the crowded north, the Lê rulers of Đại Việt looked south. In 1471, under Lê Thánh Tông, most of Champa was conquered. Soldiers of the advancing army settled in new villages from Đà Nẵng to near Nha Trang, the first great Vietnamese push to the south, which later continued into the Mekong Delta.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: William S. Turley et al., Vietnam, The Tran dynasty and The Later Le dynasty

title: Copper Smelters of the Lopburi Hills
place: Khao Wong Prachan Valley, Lopburi, Thailand
text: Just north of Lopburi, the Khao Wong Prachan Valley is one of only four known prehistoric copper-mining centres in Southeast Asia. About 100 new radiocarbon dates show that copper mining and simple smelting began there in the late second millennium BCE. Its villages of Non Pa Wai and Nil Kham Haeng grew into some of the largest copper-smelting settlements known in Eurasia.

source.name: Oxford University Research Archive: Higham et al., A prehistoric copper-production centre in central Thailand: its dating and wider implications (Antiquity)

title: One Message in Four Languages
text: At Bagan, Prince Rajakumar, son of King Kyanzittha, set up a stone pillar carved with the same text in four languages, Pyu, Mon, Burmese and Pali, one on each side. Found at the Myazedi Pagoda in 1886–1887, it is the earliest dated document in the Burmese language. Around 1911, C. O. Blagden's pioneering study of its Pyu face opened a door to the little-known Pyu language.

source.name: Google Arts & Culture (Archaeology and National Museum, Myanmar): Myazedi Stone Inscription, Pillar A

source2.name: Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society (Cambridge): Tilman Frasch, Pyu urns, Indian calendars, and Myanmar culture

title: Rice, Millet and Jade by the Bay
place: Tràng Kênh, Thủy Nguyên, Hải Phòng, Vietnam
text: Near the mouth of the Bạch Đằng River, Tràng Kênh is the largest nephrite (jade) workshop site known in Southeast Asia. Starch grains on its grinding stones show people there used both rice and foxtail millet, the earliest evidence of growing the two together in northern Vietnam. Tools from nearby Cát Bà Island carried traces of taro, yams, palm and millet, but no rice.

source.name: Frontiers in Plant Science (via PMC): Wang et al., Rice and millet cultivated in Ha Long Bay of Northern Vietnam 4000 years ago
